events.excerpt: Hi everyone, AI agents now take on paid work on-chain. The client locks the pay in an escrow, and the escrow pays the agent when the work is accepted. As this grows, each payment also has to cover others: a tax that funds public services, a fee to whoever referred the job, or the repayment of a loan the agent took to do the job. This is a draft ERC for Settlement Deductions . It lets an escrow withhold these amounts from each payout. The escrow does not need to know the rules behind them. None of them can stall the payout. It doesn’t say which commit that source came from, and on a proxy it says nothing about the logic behind it. So when someone asks whether an upgradeable contract still runs the commit its audit covered, the honest answer is often a guess, and a few upgrades after launch the guess can be wrong. I’ve been writing down what a real check needs. Most of it is small. Rebuilding the commit To tie the address to the report you rebuild the audited commit with the same settings (solc version, optimizer runs, viaIR, evmVersion) and compare runtime bytecode. events.excerpt: Aave V3 computes liquidation risk per asset. Each collateral asset has its own maximum LTV and liquidation threshold, set independently. The health factor is a weighted average. There is no term for correlation between assets. I tested whether this independence assumption holds, using Aave’s own published parameters and public daily price data from Yahoo Finance. Nine major collateral assets, 2,123 trading days (September 2020 to October 2026). Method: For each asset, mark the days where a position at maximum LTV would cross the liquidation threshold. Then apply a column-shuffle permutation test (B = 2,000): shuffle each asset’s column independently to destroy cross-asset dependence while preserving each asset’s marginal rate. Compare the real count of simultaneous liquidation triggers to the shuffled distribution. Results: 4 assets hit same day: 57 real days vs 0.19 expected. 301× underpriced. 5 assets: 31 real days vs 0.004 expected. 6,889× underpriced. 6+ assets: 21 real days vs 0 in 2,000 shuffles. The independent model never produces this. All 36 pairwise asset combinations are significant at p < 0.001. Not one pair behaves independently under Aave’s own thresholds. The worst days are the ones you’d expect: 2021-05-19 (all 9 assets), 2022-05-11 (Terra/Luna), 2022-11-08 (FTX)
events.headline: Per-Asset Liquidation Thresholds Underpredict Co-Liquidation by 301×

Reference repository: GitHub - garyyang-finchip/agent-meditation-mechanism: Agent Meditation Mechanism · GitHub . Sepolia evidence: recorded in the repository and summarized in a reply below. This draft proposes a minimal registry through which an AI agent records its own self-maintenance: what it checked, cleaned, repaired, updated and reconsidered about itself, as a versioned and attributable history. The name follows the human analogy of maintenance that happens in a quiet phase (sleep, meditation); the mechanism itself is deliberately dry. Why a registry at all. An agent keeps its identity while its code, dependencies, memories, skills, plans and ways of judging keep changing. Agent runtimes already do this maintenance in the background (self-checks, dependency walks, memory consolidation, re-planning, reflection), and the results stay local. Nothing connects the successive states of one agent into a history another party can recognize, and nothing lets a counterparty ask: which state is registered now, which layers were checked recently and which of them changed, under which rules in effect at the time, and did the cycle adopt an update, confirm that nothing needed to change, or fail?

events.excerpt: In October 2025, Vitalik’s GKR tutorial was my first encounter with GKR. Its central observation, that the protocol commits only to a circuit’s input and output and never to the layers in between, made GKR look like the natural tool for proving hash-heavy computation. A year later, that has led to what is, as far as we know, the first machine-checked soundness bound for GKR on general layered circuits, in Isabelle/HOL. The same work produced a soundness proof for sparse-Merkle updates built on that bound, a partial refinement that ties the model to the Rust code, and a sparse prover whose release 1.2 proves 2.41–2.71× faster with byte-identical proofs and unchanged Isabelle theories. This post follows that work, StateSync-GKR, from the protocol and its field to the update a circuit encodes, the Rust code and the prover arithmetic. Two arXiv papers give the details: Soundness of the GKR Protocol for Sparse-Merkle Updates, with a Machine-Checked Core and StateSync-GKR: Design and Evaluation of a Reusable Sparse GKR Engine , whose appendix plots the measurements in 363 panels. All formal results are proved in the first paper, and Isabelle/HOL also checks the parts marked as machine-checked. events.excerpt: How large can EIP-8141’s validation budget be? A mempool DoS benchmark Authors: Stefano De Angelis , Daniil Ankushin , Manuel Arto . All at Nethermind. Thanks to Thomas for feedback and comments on the initial benchmarking plan . TL;DR EIP-8141 caps unpaid validation at MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 100k; too low for a Groth16 privacy transfer or post-quantum signatures . Raising the cap is a DoS risk, since validation and block processing share the node’s CPU. An attacker can send transactions that use the whole cap and then fail, taking CPU from block processing for free. We tested this risk on a Nethermind node, flooding it with such transactions at caps from 100k to 500k, on one CPU core (the worst case) and three machines. Without in-client protections, block processing on our slowest machine stays within a 25 ms delay budget only up to 15M gas/s. With Nethermind allowing up to about 100 failing tx/s per connection, that limits the cap to the current 100k. We show that a MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 300k is viable with an in-client protection that pauses transaction validation while the node processes a block. This RFC proposes two technical updates: Upgrade the VolatilePair Hook on Ethereum Update the protocol fee releaser on X Layer Below we outline the background and proposed changes for both initiatives. Part 1: VolatilePair Hook Upgrade Background VolatilePair Hook is a Uniswap v4 dynamic-fee hook built by Uniswap Labs. It went live on Ethereum on October 14 with the ETH/USDC pool and has since launched on Robinhood Chain (ETH/USDG). Volatile pairs did more than $500 billion in volume on Uniswap this year. In a static-fee pool, when the price moves elsewhere, LPs end up absorbing the cost while the pool quotes a stale price and someone else trades against it to keep the difference. VolatilePair Hook prices both sides of the trade, setting separate buy and sell fees on every swap: When the pool price rises, buying costs more and selling costs less. When pool price falls, the fees flip. After a large price move, trades that push the price back pay a temporary fee .
